Formal quality curvilinear: a structural descriptor affecting perception of density, flow, boundary, or tone. Often scale-dependent (micro texture vs macro composition); distinct from interpretive themes.
Organisation around a centre with spokes, arcs, or concentric tendencies. Produces rotational balance and outward dispersion; common in blooms, bursts, vortices; distinct from linear flow.
High mark or element density with limited negative space. Reads as compression, pressure, or accumulation; can increase cognitive load and visual noise; distinct from sparse, airy distributions.
Low element density with ample negative space. Reads as openness, pause, or isolation; emphasises placement and interval; distinct from dense, crowded, or saturated surfaces.

Formal quality enclosed: a structural descriptor affecting perception of density, flow, boundary, or tone. Often scale-dependent (micro texture vs macro composition); distinct from interpretive themes.
Multiple strata or passes remain visible: palimpsest, accretion, or composite overlays. Encodes time and revision; can be transparent or opaque; distinct from single-pass, flat surfaces.
Broken into discontinuous parts: gaps, cuts, shards, or interrupted contours. Reads as interruption or assembly; can be collage-like or glitch-like; distinct from continuous, flowing forms.
Theme growth: an inferred emphasis that helps articulate patterns across a series—tension, drift, emergence, repair. Interpretive and revisable; distinct from purely formal descriptors.

Edges and local contrast are crisp; high spatial-frequency detail is preserved. Seen in hard ink lines, high-acutance photos, or clean vector forms; distinct from blur, haze, and soft focus.
Edges lose high-frequency detail through motion, depth-of-field, diffusion, or averaging. Produces softness and ambiguity; distinct from low-resolution pixelation, grain, or deliberate smearing.

High-frequency particulate texture: many small intensity variations at short spatial scales. Appears as film grain, high-ISO sensor noise, dithering, or sand-like stipple; distinct from smooth gradients.

Low micro-variation: gradients or planes read continuous, with minimal particulate texture. Seen in clean ink washes, polished surfaces, or compressed images; distinct from grainy, gritty, or speckled fields.
Surface with tactile variation—roughness, grain, or patterned micro-structure. Can be paper tooth, corrosion, stipple, or fabric weave; distinct from flat, uniform tone and smooth surfaces.

Single-hue or near-black-and-white palette emphasising value, texture, and structure over colour relationships. Common in ink and B/W photography; distinct from polychrome or colour-coded layers.

Formal quality polychrome: a structural descriptor affecting perception of density, flow, boundary, or tone. Often scale-dependent (micro texture vs macro composition); distinct from interpretive themes.
Digital or process error aesthetic: discontinuities, tearing, blocks, misregistration, or codec artifacts. Reads as system failure or mediation; distinct from organic irregularity and hand jitter.
Two or more layers occupy the same field, partially occluding or blending. Can be double exposure, composite drawing passes, or UI superposition; distinct from simple repetition without stacking.
